summary: Every visitor to South Sudan needs a visa: most nationalities apply online through the official eVisa portal (evisa.gov.ss) or at an embassy, with single-entry tourist visas costing around USD 100. The country remains under do-not-travel advisories from most Western governments.

vaccinations.name: Yellow fever
vaccinations.text: A yellow fever vaccination certificate (ICVP) is required if you arrive from a country with risk of transmission — which covers most regional routes into Juba — and officials often ask all arrivals for it. Vaccination is in any case strongly recommended, as South Sudan itself has yellow fever risk.

source.name: South Sudan eVisa portal — Directorate of Nationality, Passports and Immigration

vaccinations.name: Malaria prophylaxis
vaccinations.text: Malaria transmission is intense year-round throughout South Sudan. Antimalarial tablets, repellent and bed nets are strongly recommended — talk to a travel clinic before your trip.

source.name: South Sudan eVisa portal — Directorate of Nationality, Passports and Immigration

travelInsurance.text: No insurance is checked on entry, but most standard policies exclude South Sudan — visitors need specialist cover including medical evacuation, as hospital care in Juba is very limited.

source.name: South Sudan eVisa portal — Directorate of Nationality, Passports and Immigration

onwardTicket.text: Not consistently enforced, but airlines may ask for a return ticket, and most visitors travel with an invitation letter from a host organization in South Sudan.

source.name: South Sudan eVisa portal — Directorate of Nationality, Passports and Immigration

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published; immigration officers may ask about your host, accommodation and the purpose of your visit.

declarations.name: Registration with immigration
declarations.text: Foreign nationals are generally expected to register with the Directorate of Immigration in Juba within about 3 days of arrival — hotels or host organizations usually assist. Confirm current practice with your host before travel.

source.name: South Sudan eVisa portal — Directorate of Nationality, Passports and Immigration

currencyLimits.text: No reliable published threshold. Declare large sums of foreign currency on arrival to avoid difficulties on departure; taking South Sudanese pounds out of the country is restricted.

notes: Photography in public requires a permit — photographing airports, bridges, government buildings or military sites can lead to arrest even with one.
Drones and satellite phones attract close scrutiny and may be seized without prior clearance.

payments.text: South Sudan is a cash economy. Bring clean, recent US dollar notes to exchange, as cards are accepted almost nowhere and ATMs rarely work with foreign cards. The pound's street value shifts quickly, so change modest amounts at a time.

safety.text: Most governments advise against all travel to South Sudan due to armed conflict, intercommunal violence, violent crime and kidnapping. The situation can deteriorate quickly, including in Juba, and travel outside the capital requires careful planning and often armed escorts.

source.name: UK Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office — South Sudan travel advice

bestTimeToVisit.text: December to February is the heart of the dry season, when roads are passable and the heat, while intense, is at its most manageable; the rains (roughly May to October) cut off much of the country.

tips.text: South Sudan is under do-not-travel advisories from most governments — armed conflict, violent crime and kidnapping are serious risks, and the few visitors who go rely on established host organizations for security and logistics.
Never photograph in public without a government photography permit — even with one, avoid airports, bridges, checkpoints and anything official; arrests of foreigners over photos are well documented.
Register with immigration in Juba within about 3 days of arrival — your hotel or host organization can usually handle it, and missing it causes problems on departure.
Bring all the money you need as clean, recent US dollar notes. Cards and ATMs are effectively unusable, and worn or pre-2013 bills are often refused.

faq.question: Do I need a visa for South Sudan?
faq.answer: Yes — every nationality needs a visa for South Sudan. Most travelers apply online through the official eVisa portal at evisa.gov.ss (about USD 100 for a single-entry tourist visa) or at a South Sudanese embassy before travel.

faq.question: Is there a visa on arrival in South Sudan?
faq.answer: Not reliably — airlines generally require an eVisa approval or embassy visa before boarding flights to Juba. Apply online in advance rather than counting on arrangements at the airport.

faq.question: Is South Sudan safe to visit?
faq.answer: No — most governments advise against all travel due to armed conflict, intercommunal violence, crime and kidnapping. Conditions can change quickly even in Juba, and travel outside the capital needs professional security planning.

faq.question: Do I need a yellow fever certificate for South Sudan?
faq.answer: Bring one. The certificate is formally required when arriving from countries with yellow fever risk, which covers most regional routes into Juba, and officials often ask all arrivals for it. South Sudan itself has yellow fever risk, so vaccination is recommended regardless.

faq.question: Can I use the South Sudan eVisa at land borders?
faq.answer: The eVisa is designed around arrival at Juba International Airport. Land-border handling is inconsistent — if you must cross overland, get a visa from an embassy beforehand and confirm the crossing is open and considered passable.
